title: Why Teenagers Stay Up Late
context:
A. Parents often accuse teenagers of laziness, but biology offers a kinder explanation. During adolescence the body clock shifts, and the brain begins releasing melatonin, the hormone that prepares us for sleep, roughly two hours later than it does in childhood. As a result, many fifteen-year-olds do not feel drowsy until around eleven at night, however early they go to bed. Scientists stress that this is a normal developmental change rather than a flaw of character, and that it fades again in the early twenties.

B. Electronic devices are frequently blamed for late nights. In one national survey, about seven in ten teenagers admitted to using a phone while lying in bed. The blue light given off by screens is thought to delay melatonin release further, but some sleep researchers believe its role has been overstated. They argue that a thrilling video, a heated group chat or the fear of missing something online keeps the mind alert, so what teenagers watch may matter as much as the light itself.

C. Several school districts have experimented with later mornings. In one American county, the first bell was moved from 7.30 to 8.40, and researchers followed the students for two years. On average, they slept 45 minutes longer on school nights. Attendance rose, fewer pupils fell asleep in lessons, and examination results improved modestly. Critics had predicted that teenagers would simply stay up later, but the data showed that bedtimes barely changed, so the extra time in the morning became extra sleep.

D. The consequences of chronic sleep loss extend well beyond yawning in class. Teenagers who regularly sleep fewer than seven hours are more likely to report anxiety and low mood. Memory is also affected, because the brain strengthens newly learned material during deep sleep, and a shortened night leaves less time for that process. Among drivers aged seventeen to nineteen, drowsiness is a recognised factor in road accidents, particularly in the early hours of the morning and late in the afternoon.

E. Many adolescents try to repay their sleep debt at weekends. Sleeping until noon on Saturday and Sunday, however, pushes the body clock later still, so that getting up on Monday feels like flying across several time zones. Researchers call this mismatch between the school-week and weekend rhythms 'social jet lag'. Although a long lie-in brings temporary relief, studies suggest it does not fully repair the damage caused by a week of short nights, and the benefits for attention and mood are only partial.

F. Doctors suggest a few practical habits. Keeping the same bedtime and wake-up time every day helps to steady the body clock, and opening the curtains to bright daylight soon after waking helps to anchor it. Drinks containing caffeine are best avoided after midday, since the stimulant can linger in the body for many hours. Yet schools that wish to start later often meet resistance, because sports fixtures and bus timetables are arranged around the existing day and would be costly to change.
